content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to study the effect of changing natural image attributes such as pose, position, background, lighting and size in current state of the art vision models. The authors create a dataset for their experiments by placing 3d warehouse objects in non-uniform backgrounds. They then examine the effect of variation of the aforementioned factors using standard tools such as fine-tuning and linear evaluation. The models under consideration are wide ranging including MAE, CLIP, ViTs and ResNets.

Model generalization is compared by contrasting accuracy for canonical settings (most common values for image attributes) with accuracy obtained by varying one or more factors in the image. 

The major findings are:
1. SOTA pertained models trained with little factor variability exhibit low robustness towards factor variation.
2. Architecture changes, training paradigm seem to matter little when it comes to robustness whereas more training data seems to help robustness (confirming previous work).
3. Increasing the amount of variation of instances of a single factor improves robustness to that factor. Additionally, increasing variation for one factor seems to affect robustness for other factors.
4. Factor variation within a class can help generalization in other, closely-related classes too but degrades generalization in dissimilar classes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The papers objectives and conclusions are clearly stated and, on the whole, the paper is fairly clear.
2. The authors have done a great job in performing an exhaustive set of experiments to test their hypothesis.
3.  Significance: Understanding blind spots in large SOTA models is an extremely important problem as they are deployed in the real world.
4. Novelty of the problem: From what I know, decomposing images into factors and then varying them independently to study effects of variations has not been studied (at least for models such as MAE in conjunction with ViTs etc)

Weaknesses:
1. My main concern with the paper is that many of the results in the paper seem “obvious”. We already have results showing how more data seems to help generalization (Radford et al, which to be fair the authors have cited)  or that some attributes are more important to generalization than other attribute (at least for ViTs and CNNs) i.e. pose vs position gaps being substantially different.
2. Related to the previous point, when the authors do find certain interesting properties like the fact that MAEs seem to be significantly affected by position and color, there is no analysis about why something like might happen. The authors instead give (a very plausible) explanation without any evidence. A deeper analysis of many of the points brought up in the paper would elevate the paper significantly.
3. The effect sizes measured in many experiments are relatively small. For example, in the experiment which tries to measure the effect of variation in one factor affecting another, averages effects are in the 1-3% range. I’m not sure how significant observations are.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The problem of understanding large SOTA models is significant and the approach is sufficiently novel. The paper is well written and clear for the most part (see below). The relative lack of novelty in results has been pointed out above.

A terminology thing that distracted me: What is the difference a sample, an instance and a class? I would have assumed a sample and an instance would mean the same thing but the following statement “we ensure a particular fraction of samples per instance feature diverse values (i.e., departing from canonical) ” left me confused. Elsewhere it is said “across three settings: 1) when all samples vary 2) when only some instances vary 3) when only some classes vary”.  Am I correct in interpreting the word samples in the first statement in the probabilistic sense of the word? Or am I missing something?
content.summary_of_the_review: I’d like to thank the authors for a comprehensive analysis of such a wide variety of models. I think the evaluation is rigorous and the conclusions are well supported. High quality empiricism is very important for our field. However, I think this paper is much more about the ‘what’ than the ‘how’ or ‘why’ at the moment and, therefore, does not in my view exhibit a sufficient advance in our understanding as field to warrant publication. I acknowledge some of this review is a matter of taste in research and I hope the authors understand my point of view.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the robustness of SOTA computer vision models by measuring how much each model is affected by perturbed input images under a combination of pose, position background, lighting color, and size variations. The models considered in the study include a wide range of models such as ViT, CLIP MLPMixer, SimCLR, etc. Experimental results suggest that augmentation in one factor helps with robustness in other factors, but poorly generalizes across classes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

* Extensive experiments with SOTA vision models. Selection of the SOTA vision models are comprehensive and has a good coverage spanning fully supervised SOTA models, as well as self-supervised models, with representative architectures. 
* Experiments include many different combinations of input variations to tease apart one effect from another and are well controlled.


Weakness

* Paper writing is very hard to follow and does not read well. There are lots of grammatical errors and poorly structured sentences with many repetitions. 
* Experiments are somewhat expected and most of them do not not add too much value to prior art.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper lacks clarity in terms of the writing and is hard to read. Experiments are well executed but its findings are rather trivial and not too original.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is an experiment-focused paper and studies an important problem of robustness in computer vision. Although a lot of experiments have been conducted in this work, considering the lack of originality and clarity, I would not recommend it for acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a dataset that contains objects of different classes set against backgrounds, where the background can vary along with other aspects of the object such as its size, position, lighting, and pose. Using this dataset, the paper evaluates a suite of pretrained modern image classification models (fine-tuned or with linear adaptation to the new dataset) to measure their robustness to variations in each of these factors (pose, lighting, size, etc.). Using this methodology, the paper finds substantial sensitivity of these models to these types of variation, and measures the extent to which training with different variations can mitigate this sensitivity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The dataset introduced in the paper might be useful to other researchers as a controlled testbed to study these sorts of variations.
- The characterization of how much training with one type of variation/augmentation benefits robustness to other forms of variation is potentially useful, as is the characterization of how much and what type of training augmentation/variation is necessary to close robustness gaps.

Weaknesses:
- Many of these results are already known or easily inferred from prior work, which has shown that models are very sensitive to distribution shifts of many kinds, that data augmentation can help robustness but only if the augmented data is sufficiently similar to the test-time data, and that robustness to one type of data shift does not necessarily imply robustness to other shifts.
- Relatedly, some prior work is missing. This is not a comprehensive list, but for example https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15831 studies the effect of fine-tuning on OOD robustness, and https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04649 examines the robustness gap for many models on many distribution shifts, both natural and synthetic. 
- Some of the explanations/claims don't seem to be supported by the data in the figures/tables, unless I'm missing something. In particular, I don't see how the plots in Figure 2 support the claim made in the caption (I do see that supervised models tend to do better than self-supervised ones, but the improvement doesn't seem consistently better for fine-tuned models). Another example of this is the last sentence on page 5, which claims that "fine-tuning also led to less variance in accuracy drops across models"--but this is not true for the case of varying background, shown in Figure 3. 
- Perhaps I do not fully understand the dataset being introduced, but from the description it sounds like particular, sometimes random combinations of factor variations are included while others are excluded, for the case of examples with multiple factors varying. My concern is that this might limit the flexibility of the dataset for future researchers, who might want to customize exactly which combinations of variations they study. Why not instead release a framework that enables researchers to generate their own images by selecting the desired factors?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: suggestions for improvement
- Although the writing is generally clear, there are enough typos (repeated or missing words, missing commas, etc.) that it's too long to list here. 
- The text in the figures is too small to read comfortably without zooming in.
- Lots of data is presented tabularly, or in very complex/small figures (e.g. Fig 6) that would be easier to understand if it were presented visually. Perhaps consider a similar plot format to the one used in https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04649, which compares the robustness gaps among many models in a single figure, and is easy to visually understand. This would also address another concern I have with Figure 6, which is that the baseline accuracies are not shown, which makes the robustness gaps difficult to interpret.
- Figure 1 is unclear. It's basically a table, but without enough explanation as to what each column refers to, particularly for the last column (which is referenced at the bottom of page 7, but still not explained what exactly it's measuring). For each column, it needs to be clear exactly what was done during training and what the number reported is measuring.
- In Figures 2, 3, 4 the same y axis bounds are used for all subfigures. I understand this was probably done to make the absolute placement of each figure clear, but it has the unfortunate side effect of making the figures difficult to read for those factors that do not suffer large generalization gaps, where the data are all very close together.
- The last paragraph in section 5.2 would, I believe, be better placed close to Figure 3, since they discuss similar experiments.

Quality and Novelty
- I do think there is some novelty in the breadth of transformations or "factors" considered, and the set of models, but I'm not sure how valuable it is given that as far as I can tell all of the results are already known for very similar situations (slightly different models and data shifts, or subsets of these models/data shifts). Certainly having the full results is nice, but I'm not sure how impactful it will be.

Reproducibility
- I would expect the authors to release code and data or data-generating code, but based on the description in the paper I don't think there should be any issues with reproducibility (modulo code/data release, and clarifications about some of the experiments as described above under Clarity).
content.summary_of_the_review: I do agree with the authors that the problem of out-of-distribution robustness (or lack thereof) is of great importance in machine learning, and that much remains to be understood. I believe there is some value to the proposed dataset and experiments, but I have substantial concerns about the clarity of the presentation and the novelty of the experiments (especially given the relatively sparse related work discussion) that make me doubt the impact the paper would have.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper seeks to empirically validate the robustness of common vision models to controlled changes in lighting, pose, position background, and size. They introduce a synthetic dataset composited with natural images to measure the effects of these factors. They show that in these settings, common models show a lack of robustness _during training_.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
##### Strengths

- Interesting and very relevant problem. Findings are unsurprising (e.g. more diverse data helps) mostly but still good to know. The fact that diversity in some factors helps performance on others is also interesting.
- The choice of models and pretraining data is sufficiently diverse across many scales.

##### Weaknesses

- It's well known that finetuning CLIP reduces robustness. You should evaluate CLIP zero-shot performance on these object categories. You could also see how [1] works in this setting. Would also be interesting to see this data in scatter-plot format.
- Could use a more thorough explanation of the controlled distribution shifts. I didn't see an ablation across different factor settings (e.g. less pose variation between train and OOD test)
- It's unclear how well these synthetic results generalize to real datasets. Do you have any controlled real experiments to show that these results transfer?


[1] Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models, Wortsman et al. 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

Experiments are clear and well-thought out. The experimental setup needs some more explaining however, in particular, please elucidate how you chose the distribution shift for your factors of variation. "Chosen arbitrarily" is a bit too vague.

**Quality**

No complaints about writing quality. Some of the plots, however, are hard to read. Could use more colorblind friendly color palettes.

**Reproducibility**

No code was provided, reproducibility seems good however. Could use more details on dataset construction (e.g. distribution of factors of variation).

**Novelty**

The novelty is mostly in the experimentation against new models. The additions versus Alcorn et al. are mostly in introducing new factors of variatin.
content.summary_of_the_review:
_weak reject_

The paper and experiments are interesting. However, there are two main factors which result in my rating:

1. Lack of CLIP zero-shot numbers. 
2. Can we trust that these results are valid on real datasets? This is necessary to validate the synthetic benchmark.


[1] Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models, Wortsman et al. 2020

content.title: The Robustness Limits of SoTA Vision Models to Natural Variation
content.TL;DR: Even today's best vision models are not robust and struggle to generalize changes in factors such as pose, size, and position.
content.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art vision models introduced new architectures, learning paradigms, and larger pretraining data, leading to impressive performance on tasks such as classification. While previous generations of vision models were shown to lack robustness to factors such as pose, it’s unclear the extent to which this next generation of models are more robust. To study this question, we develop a dataset of more than 7 million images with controlled changes in pose, position, background, lighting, and size. We study not only how robust recent state-of-the-art models are, but also the extent to which models can generalize variation in factors when they’re present during training. We consider a catalog of recent vision models, including vision transformers (ViT), self-supervised models such as masked autoencoders (MAE), and models trained on larger datasets such as CLIP. We find out-of-the-box, even today’s best models are not robust to common changes in pose, size, and background. When some samples varied during training, we found models required a significant portion of diversity to generalize—though eventually robustness did improve. When diversity is only seen for some classes however, we found models did not generalize to other classes, unless the classes were very similar to those seen varying during training. We hope our work will shed further light on the blind spots of SoTA models and spur the development of more robust vision models
